The extensions largely preserve an output-shifting operation, and several MMLU subjects and cipher offsets show little successful adaptation. Shared-head ablations establish component reuse more directly than reuse of the complete proposed algorithm. The base-8 error patterns likewise do not establish the specific internal conditional algorithm in Listing 1.

Robustness of circuit selection is insufficiently characterized. Most analyses use 100 prompts; discovery uses four-shot prompts with 33% accuracy, whereas the main validation uses sixteen-shot prompts with 86% accuracy. A clear held-out discovery/validation split, variation across demonstration samples and prompt formats, and uncertainty on circuit-recovery estimates would make the conclusions more reliable.

strengths: The controlled counterfactual task provides a useful setting for studying compositional in-context learning. Excluding demonstrated test answers helps distinguish function application from direct answer copying.

Head-output interventions reveal heterogeneous contributions that change with the requested offset. Replication in additional models, especially Llama-3 and Mistral, and interventions across arithmetic and letter-shifting tasks provide meaningful evidence of component reuse.

The appendices provide substantial supporting analysis, including circuit evaluation, threshold sensitivity, alternative ablations, and informative failure cases. Model identifiers, head lists, prompts, and computational requirements support reproducibility; code and data release is reported.

The experiments establish causal involvement more convincingly than they establish that previous-token heads encode an expected-versus-observed discrepancy or that individual FI heads implement distinct functional pieces. Appendix D reports 78.4% recovery of the normalized logit gap, with the circuit’s mean logit difference favoring the base answer (+0.56), unlike the full model (-1.26). Local search improves recovery to 89%, but introduces heads outside the proposed three-group account. Reporting recovered task accuracy and validating the expanded circuit would clarify explanatory sufficiency.

The distinction from existing function-vector and false-induction mechanisms needs stronger experimental support. Non-overlap with ten previously reported FV heads, selected using different tasks, does not establish a distinct mechanism. Matched comparisons between single-step offset tasks and composed addition-plus-offset tasks would better isolate the novel contribution.

Generalization remains restricted to shifting operations, and several extensions are weak: Caesar cipher is limited to individual characters, shifted-MMLU performance varies substantially across subjects, and base-8 accuracy is only 14–16% in the carry cases. Llama-2’s approximately +2 intervention effect and 6% off-by-one accuracy also qualify the cross-model universality claim.

Most central analyses use 100 prompts, without clear independent discovery/validation splits or uncertainty estimates for circuit membership and faithfulness. Discovery also uses four-shot prompts with 33% accuracy, whereas much validation uses sixteen-shot prompts with 86% accuracy. Stability across independently sampled prompts, shot counts, and successful versus unsuccessful examples would strengthen confidence.

The evaluation extends beyond one model and one offset: six models receive behavioral evaluation, four receive mechanistic analysis, and interventions across arithmetic, shifted QA, and cipher tasks provide evidence of component reuse. The empirical investigation is substantial: behavioral evaluation covers six models, circuit analysis covers four, and additional experiments examine several offsets and task families. Intervention heatmaps reveal complementary, offset-dependent contributions from individual heads.

Appendix C.4.2 identifies important MLP contributions that remain unexplained. Interventions independently manipulating the hypothesized intermediate sum and discrepancy would strengthen the mechanistic account.
